sections.html:
• Name: Vampire shrimp (Atya gabonensis)
  • Optimal tank size: 70 litres
  • Breeding: Very difficult
  • Optimal KH: 2–15
  • Optimal TDS: 150–200 (100–300)
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: Detritivore/omnivore
  • Temperament: Peaceful
  • Colour: greyish, whitish, light blue to reddish-brown, strong blue

Vampire shrimp (Atya gabonensis) are very peaceful and incredibly shy despite their enormous size and formidable appearance. Once acclimated, they are relatively easy to care for. Unlike most shrimp, they are filter feeders, so a flow must be provided in the tank. They are very hard to breed, but this is compensated by an extremely long lifespan.

The species is harvested on a small scale in northern Nigeria and elsewhere in West Africa. Atya gabonensis is on the list of threatened species. The pet industry depends completely on wild-caught animals.
Common in West Africa and first reported in Gabon. Harvested in northern Nigeria and elsewhere in West Africa.

Their natural history is not well documented. They inhabit mangrove environments, in available boles, crevices and root masses of the Cross River system.

Mangrove leaf litter provides an important nutrient base for food webs. During its decomposition many nutrients are released and detritus is formed, which also serves as an essential nursery ground for juveniles.

Vampire shrimp need a relatively big tank because of their unique feeding behaviour. 70 litres is the minimum tank size to keep them comfortably. They are quite social and do not mind being crowded, so a 70-litre tank will comfortably house 4–5 shrimp.

Do not try to keep Vampire shrimp in absolutely clean water. In the wild they prefer muddy, mangrove or sandy-mud bottom habitats. The tank should be well cycled and rich in microorganisms. Careful acclimation is needed, as with all shrimp.

Shrimp are shy and like hiding places, preferring tight-fitting shelters. Once they find the best spot they never use any other. If they outgrow their home they may dig a burrow to enlarge it. Shelters are especially important after moulting, when they are vulnerable; while the new exoskeleton hardens they sit there all the time, so provide hiding places large enough to conceal the whole body.

Exoskeletons contain a lot of minerals and proteins. Do not remove moulted shells if you keep Vampire shrimp with dwarf shrimp: Vampires cannot eat their moults, but other shrimp will gladly do it.

Some aquarists recommend never doing maintenance while they are out of their hiding spots, as it can scare them so much that they hide for days.

Vampire shrimp prefer pH variations from 6.6 to 7.1, corresponding to the dry and rainy seasons in their natural habitat. They thrive in warm temperatures, 22–28°C, and do not tolerate temperatures as low as those most dwarf shrimp enjoy.

A sand substrate is preferable. It will not damage their delicate fans, and they also consume some sand: sand was found in 95.2% of specimens studied. It is not known why; perhaps sand is part of the detritus or helps digestion. They can be fine with a rock or gravel substrate.

A moderate water current is crucial. It can be provided by installing a secondary pump near or on the bottom, which suits Vampire shrimp better. Make sure the tank is adequately aerated.

For filtration, a sponge (Matten) filter or similar is recommended.

To watch their nocturnal activity, a night-glow bulb or similar can be used.

Vampire shrimp are active filter feeders. They use their fans (plume-like bristles) to filter the water column and also scrape the substrate for food. They are omnivorous-detritivores. In stomach studies, algae and organic detritus were the major constituents (61.9% of items by number), followed by diatoms (20.9%) and insect parts (1.9%, mostly eaten by large shrimp). Green algae was the most preferred food. Algae were the most consumed item in small shrimp (2.0–5.9 cm, 86%), medium (6.0–10.9 cm, 60%) and large (11.0–14.0 cm, 47%). Organic detritus was found in all size groups.

In the aquarium they need microscopic food particles. Powdered food dropped into the current is ideal: phytoplankton, zooplankton, fine foods such as Hikari First Bites, New Life Spectrum Small Fry starter, Golden Pearls (5–50 micron), dried nettle leaves, spinach powder.

Some keepers advise green water, dense enough that you cannot see your hand through a soda bottle full of it. Feed enough to turn the water slightly hazy. It is better to turn the filter off for an hour or so while feeding, leaving a secondary pump running to keep the food suspended; otherwise the food may be filtered out before it reaches their fans, unless you pipette-feed in front of them.

Do not give regular flakes, wafers or pellets, which take too long to dissolve; if nothing else is available, grind them to powder first.

Flakes or pellets can be ground in a coffee grinder to about the texture of baby powder, which is also a good way to combine different foods. If kept with fish, feed at night, otherwise they rarely get enough. Picking detritus with their fans does not necessarily mean they are hungry, but if they do it very often, give more food. Calcium plays a huge role for shrimp.

Vampire shrimp are extremely shy and hide almost all the time. Unlike Bamboo shrimp, they usually choose feeding spots on the ground near hiding places, so shelter must be provided. Once they have found a comfortable spot in the current they prefer not to move much.

They do well in groups, often crowded close together. They are 100% peaceful: they have no claws and can only push and poke with their fans, so they cannot harm anybody. They are predominantly twilight and nocturnal and are rarely seen in the daytime.

The name comes from the most popular theory: they lurk in the tank at night and have spikes on their feet that look like fangs or claws.

Tankmates: they can be kept with any dwarf shrimp (Cherry, Snowball, Ghost, Amano, Bamboo, etc.) without risk of crossbreeding, and with any snails. Because of their size they are kept with small fish that might still endanger dwarf shrimp (guppies, cherry barbs, dwarf chain loaches, Sawbwa resplendens, strawberry rasboras, etc.). Do not keep them with big or aggressive fish, crabs or crayfish; they are defenceless and become a quick meal when they moult.

Males and females cannot be told apart as juveniles. Once about 5–6 cm long sexual dimorphism begins to show, and at 7–8 cm or more the difference is quite prominent.

  1. Size: males are larger than females.
  2. Abdominal plates: females have larger abdominal plates at the start of the abdomen; the shell is rounder and deeper through the belly.
  3. First pair of legs: males have thicker first legs, particularly in the second segment behind the main leg joint, which also has very prominent bristles.

In young Vampire shrimp the difference is harder to see because females also have thick legs.

Only two successful breedings in captivity are known. Larvae take a long time to develop into tiny copies of the adults and can do so only in saltwater. In the wild, fecundity varied with female size: 850–12,220 eggs in females of 6.5–11 cm. Reproductive activity peaked in the rainy season. They always moult before mating, when the female cuticle is soft.

Breeding setup (German breeders, crustahunter.com): 60-litre tank; Dennerle gravel; Liquizell and live phytoplankton as food (later a coarser fluid Artemia food); marine salt to prepare brackish water (28–30 g/l); constant parameters pH 7.6–8.0, GH 21, KH 10–15, NO2 0, NO3 0. The tank was cycled for four weeks, with lights on at least 11 hours a day so that bacteria and algae develop for larval survival.

After mating the female carries the eggs for 3–4 weeks. After hatching, move the larvae into saltwater as fast as possible; they cannot tolerate freshwater for long, and the adult female can catch and kill most larvae with her fans. Larvae can be siphoned out into brackish water.

Feed larvae right after moving them. Phytoplankton is the main food for 3 weeks, dosed generously four times a day with a pipette. In the fourth week add a coarser fluid food. Provide plenty of light (10–12 h) to grow algae, and keep adding a little powdered food. Some larvae always died.

In the first weeks larvae swim head-down and cannot control their movement. Then colour changes to reddish-brown or bluish and they swim horizontally, active at night. It takes 3 months to reach the post-larval stage, developing pleopods and small fans. At about 4 months a small dark spot (the innards) shows in the neck, meaning the transformation into tiny adults is complete and they can be moved to freshwater. Larval development took almost 4 months, though another report gave 33–44 days.

Transition to freshwater, never suddenly: 1) Half fill a container with brackish water from the breeding tank and add the young shrimp. 2) Slowly add freshwater from the destination tank, as in drip acclimation. 3) Wait until the freshwater is double the amount of brackish water. 4) Leave for 24 hours, aerated. 5) Move to the freshwater tank.

Appearance: heavily built. In the wild they reach 12–15 cm; in captivity usually not more than 9–11 cm. They use modified chelipeds to collect fine particles from the bottom or filter them from flowing water. The life cycle includes marine larval and post-larval stages.

Colour varies from greyish, whitish, light blue to reddish-brown to strong blue and may change slightly with each moult. Colour also depends on age and environment; a dark substrate intensifies it, and with age it can fade to reddish-brown shades, which dominate in this species. They can lose some colour after a moult, but it returns.

They can live 8–10 years with proper care. They grow slowly and do not moult often; Bamboo shrimp usually outgrow them at the same age, but eventually Vampire shrimp become larger.

Some keepers believe that too few minerals can make them whitish or reddish; this is unproven.
